newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Unrest clips gains on Israel bond market.
newsitem.headline: Unrest clips gains on Israel bond market.

text.p: Israeli bond prices closed up on Sunday but traders said the gains would have been higher if not for the political uncertainty and the falling stock market.
* Consumer price index (CPI) linked government bonds: +0.1 pct 166.78
* Dollar linked government bonds: +0.8 pct to 163.46
* Unlinked government bonds (Gilon - issued for 4 years): unchanged at 164.41.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: unchanged at 156.72

"The gains were small, mainly influenced by the decline in the stock market...Everything is affected by the general atmosphere," said an investment manager. "The bond market would have risen more had the atmosphere not been bad."
Gidi Halpern of Meitav Investment and Securities said most of the demand was for CPI- and dollar-linked bonds.

"There are expectations for a depreciation in the shekel tomorrow following the strengthening of the dollar on Friday. Expectations are that tomorrow there will be big demand for dollar-linked bonds. Already today there was a sharp rise in these bonds," he said.
The demand for CPI-linked bonds had risen following a rise in inflationary expectations, he said.

"Inflationary expectations have risen because of the depreciation and because government spending will go up to finance the fighting with the Palestinians. When inflation is expected to rise, demand for CPI-linked bonds rises," he said.

He added that prices of eight-month Makam bills had fallen by about 0.1 percent because investors were switching to CPI-linked and dollar-linked bonds. "There is a tendency to switch from unlinked bonds and Makams to CPI and dollar-linked bonds," he said.
The bloody clashes of the past few days between Israeli and Palestinian forces, in which nearly 70 people have been killed, have caused stock prices to fall.
Note: Makam bills are zero-coupon unlinked certificates issued for periods ranging from three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues the Makams to absorb money from the public.
The Tel Aviv bourse closed two hours early on Sunday and will do so throughout the week due to the Jewish holiday of Succoth. Normal trading hours will resume on October 6.
